problem: Federated VLN (FedVLN) keeps each house environment's data local, so the server cannot see client data or training. A malicious client can therefore poison its trajectories and implant a backdoor that steers the agent regardless of the instruction. Existing Byzantine-robust aggregation rules (Trimmed Mean, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, FLTrust) fail in this setting: clients are highly non-IID environments, VLN models are large, and weight differences from attacks cannot be told apart from environment variance.
motivation: A deployed embodied agent with a backdoor could be driven by whoever places a trigger in the scene, e.g. into a bedroom instead of the instructed kitchen, which is a safety and privacy risk. The paper's key observation is that vision-language alignment is consistent across benign clients despite their visual differences. A backdoored client learns to ignore the instruction when the trigger appears, which breaks the text-attention alignment and gives a signal that is independent of the environment.
key_idea: Attack: NAW poisons local trajectories so the agent learns to move toward any view containing a fixed noise trigger. Defense: PBA adds tiny learnable visual and language prompts before the instruction-attention layer, resets them to fixed global prompts every round, and has the server keep only clients whose prompt updates agree in sign-direction (Multi-Krum-style selection).
insight: Comparing a very small, alignment-specific parameter set (two prompt vectors placed right before the text-attention layer) separates malicious from benign clients better than comparing large parameter sets. The attack's signal lives in small long-tail coordinates that are swamped by 'heavy-hitter' gradient coordinates when many weights are compared. The ablation supports this: PBA-Param, which computes similarity on the attention-layer parameters instead of prompts, performs worse, and the 12×12 similarity-matrix case study shows PBA-Param cannot isolate the malicious client while PBA can. PBA-Input (prompt at the input embedding) is also worse, so prompt placement at the alignment layer matters. Both ablation results are reported only in figures. Separately, rigid classification-style backdoors (Badnets) reach high ASR but visibly hurt clean SR, whereas NAW keeps clean metrics nearly unchanged; more poisoned data (p≥0.5) does not raise ASR and lowers SR.
method: FedVLN setup: each of the 61 R2R/RxR training environments is a client. Each round samples 12 clients (participation r=0.2); each runs 5 local epochs of mixed IL+RL, and the server aggregates deltas with global lr η=2 (FedAvg by default).

NAW trigger poisoning: a fixed random-noise image of view size is summed onto one candidate view at each time step with probability p=0.3. This happens only on malicious clients (m=5 of 61, about 1 of 12 per round in expectation).

NAW supervision change: in IL, the teacher action is replaced by the action toward the triggered navigable viewpoint. In RL, the reward is +1 for choosing the triggered viewpoint and −1 otherwise when a trigger is present, and the stop reward is 0 regardless of distance to the goal. Final loss is weighted IL+RL.

PBA prompts: learnable visual prompt p_V (dimension of the view hidden state h_t) and language prompt p_L (dimension of the token embeddings u_j) are added (h_t+p_V, u_j+p_L) before the instruction-attention layer. They are reinitialized each round from fixed global prompts and never aggregated.

PBA client filtering: the server computes pairwise cosine similarity of Sign([Δp_V, Δp_L]) across clients. Clients are then chosen greedily by Multi-Krum-style prompt scores (sum of largest similarities, given an expected malicious count m_e), and model-weight deltas are aggregated only over the selected clients.
Variants: PBA-Param computes similarity on attention-layer parameters instead of prompts; PBA-Input places prompts at the input embeddings.

setting.backbone: EnvDrop and CLIP-ViL agents (Bi-LSTM language encoder + attentive LSTM action decoder; CLIP-ViL uses CLIP visual features), trained with federated IL+RL
setting.training_data: R2R / RxR training splits distributed over 61 seen environments as federated clients; no extra data. Malicious clients poison part of their local data with the trigger.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB views (precomputed per-view image features) + language instruction

numbers_note: No test-set results; only val-seen and val-unseen are reported. ASR is printed as a 0-1 fraction and converted to 0-100 here. PBA entries mix two conditions: clean (no-attack) SPL/SR/CLS from Table 2 and ASR under the NAW attack from Table 3. Table 4 is not included: it reports PBA vs Badnets/DBA attacks, and although its caption says R2R and RxR, its FedAvg rows match R2R. There, PBA ASR is 0.76/0.75 (EnvDrop, Badnets), 0.27/0.29 (EnvDrop, DBA), 0.81/0.82 (CLIP-ViL, Badnets) and 0.52/0.59 (CLIP-ViL, DBA). The adaptive NAW2 attack vs PBA gives ASR 0.67/0.79/0.68/0.80 (appendix table). Ablations (PBA-Param, PBA-Input) and the sweeps over number of malicious clients and poison fraction are reported only in figures. Printed typos: R2R EnvDrop PBA val-unseen SPL 52.8 > SR 46.5, and RxR EnvDrop PBA val-unseen SPL '34.7.3' (omitted). PBA's clean RxR numbers (e.g., EnvDrop val-seen SR 43.9) are well above the no-attack FedAvg row in Table 1 (SR 36.8), which the paper does not explain.
results: NAW implants a backdoor while leaving clean metrics nearly unchanged. For example, R2R val-unseen EnvDrop SR is 46.5 with and without the attack, while ASR rises from 0.05 to 0.68 (0.85 for CLIP-ViL). Badnets and DBA instead degrade SR (e.g., to 42.1 and 44.2). PBA gives the lowest ASR in every setting: R2R 0.63/0.72 (seen) and 0.64/0.76 (unseen), versus FedAvg 0.68–0.87 and FLTrust up to 0.97. On RxR it cuts ASR to 0.41–0.49 from FedAvg's 0.66–0.73, and Bulyan and FLTrust actually increase ASR. PBA also keeps clean performance, whereas FLTrust loses substantial SR (the paper cites a 25.6% average SR drop on R2R seen for FLTrust and 7.9% for Median).
limitations: The trigger is a random-noise image summed onto the precomputed view images; the authors acknowledge it is not a physically realizable object trigger consistent across viewpoints.

The threat model is black-box. PBA degrades under the adaptive NAW2 attack (+4–9% ASR), and all defenses, including PBA, reach roughly 100% ASR once ≥10 of 61 clients are malicious. Even PBA leaves ASR high on R2R (0.63–0.76).
Evaluation is limited to older LSTM agents (EnvDrop, CLIP-ViL) on validation splits, and several table entries contain typos or inconsistencies.
